_about: Hand-authored target-standard rewrites for the worst-scoring descriptions, merged into reports/explanations.json by tools/analyse_explanations.py under `summary.examples_of_rewrites`. The original is always read back out of the database, never from this file, so a rewrite cannot claim to have improved text that has since changed.
_selection: 148 problems tie at the floor score of 10. These 10 are the first by slug. The tie is not an accident: every one of the 148 has an empty or comment-only function_signature and the single example line `- input {} -> 'result'`, so there is no problem statement to be specific about and the rewrite has to supply one.
_house_style: Name the function and its parameters with types, state the return contract, name the edge cases explicitly, and give worked examples with real inputs and real expected outputs. Length is a consequence, not a target -- the library's median description is 317 characters and a good one is often shorter than a bad one.

rewrites.notes: Title promises a text transformation; the row supplies a signature of `def solve(a, b): return a or b` and a test that expects the string 'result'. The rewrite is a specification to implement, not a description of existing behaviour, and the signature and both tests have to be replaced with it.
rewrites.rewrite:
Acronym Transformer

Implement `to_acronym(phrase)`.

Split `phrase` on whitespace and return the uppercase first character of each word joined together, with no spaces or separators.

Rules:
- `phrase` is a string and may contain any number of spaces, tabs or newlines between words. Split on whitespace and ignore empty runs, so leading, trailing and repeated spaces never produce empty letters.
- Preserve the original word order.
- Only the first character of each word is used; the rest of the word is discarded, so `to_acronym('Parameterized')` is `'P'`, not `'PAR'`.
- Uppercase using `str.upper()` on that character. A word beginning with a digit or punctuation keeps that character as-is -- `to_acronym('3D printing')` is `'3P'`.
- Return `""` (the empty string) when `phrase` contains no non-whitespace characters.
- Return the value; do not print it.

Edge cases:
- `''` and `'   '` both return `''`.
- A single word returns that word's first character uppercased.

Examples:
- `to_acronym('Portable Network Graphics')` returns `'PNG'`
- `to_acronym('  Asynchronous   JavaScript  and XML ')` returns `'AJAX'`
- `to_acronym('Application Programming Interface')` returns `'API'`
- `to_acronym('hypertext markup language')` returns `'HML'`, not `'HTML'`. The embedded capitals in `HyperText` do not produce a second letter, because only the first character of each word is read
- `to_acronym('3D printing')` returns `'3P'`
- `to_acronym('   ')` returns `''`

rewrites.notes: No signature, and a single example that reads `input {} -> 'result'`. The row is one of 148 in this state. Everything below -- the two-space gutter, the pad-short-row rule, the no-truncation rule -- is a decision the rewrite makes explicitly so that a student's output can be checked character for character.
rewrites.rewrite:
Alignment Formatter Pro

Implement `align_columns(rows)`.

`rows` is a list of lists of strings. Pad every row on the right with empty strings so all rows are the same length, then left-align each column by padding each cell with trailing spaces to that column's widest cell across the whole table. Join the cells of a row with exactly two spaces and return the list of formatted rows, preserving the input order.

Rules:
- The gutter between columns is two spaces, and no other spacing is inserted. A cell is padded on the right only -- never on the left.
- Column widths are computed across the entire table, not per row, so every returned line has the same length: the sum of the column widths plus two spaces per column boundary. A row with no columns returns the empty string.
- Ragged input is the normal case, not an error: a short row is padded with empty strings to the length of the longest row before widths are measured.
- `widths[i]` is the length of the longest entry in column `i`. Cells shorter than that get trailing spaces; cells of exactly that length get none.
- Return an empty list when `rows` is empty.
- Do not strip leading or trailing whitespace that is part of a cell's own content, and do not print.

Edge cases:
- `[]` returns `[]`.
- `[[]]` returns `['']` -- one row, zero columns, joined to nothing.
- `[['a', 'bbb'], ['cc', 'd']]` returns `['a   bbb', 'cc  d  ']`.

Examples:
- `align_columns([['name', 'score'], ['ada', '100'], ['linus', '7']])` returns `['name   score', 'ada    100  ', 'linus  7    ']`
- `align_columns([['a', 'bb'], ['cccc']])` returns `['a     bb', 'cccc    ']`
- `align_columns([])` returns `[]`

The rewrite specifies the directive grammar precisely because `apache2.conf` has real edge cases (continuation lines, `<VirtualHost *:80>` blocks, quoted values) and a student cannot be graded against an unstated subset of them.
rewrites.rewrite:
Apache Config Parser

Implement `parse_directives(text)`.

`text` is the whole contents of an Apache-style configuration file. Return a dict mapping each directive name to its value, lowercasing the name and stripping surrounding whitespace from both.

Rules:
- A directive is a line of the form `Name value`. Split on the first run of whitespace only, so the value may itself contain spaces: `DocumentRoot /var/www/html` gives `'documentroot'` -> `'/var/www/html'`.
- Skip blank lines and lines whose first non-whitespace character is `#`.
- A line with a name but no value gives that name the empty string `''`.
- If a name appears more than once, the last occurrence wins. Do not accumulate into a list.
- Section markers (`<VirtualHost *:80>`, `</VirtualHost>`) and indented continuation lines are out of scope for this problem: treat every non-comment, non-blank line as a directive, including section markers, and return them as keys with `''` as the value.
- Return an empty dict for input that contains only comments and blank lines.
- Return the dict; do not print it.

Edge cases:
- `''` returns `{}`.
- Tabs as well as spaces separate the name from the value.
- A trailing comment on a value line is part of the value: `Port 8080 # the public port` gives `'port'` -> `'8080 # the public port'`.

Examples:
- `parse_directives('# config\nServerRoot /etc/httpd\nListen 80\n')` returns `{'serverroot': '/etc/httpd', 'listen': '80'}`
- `parse_directives('Port 8080\nPort 9090\n')` returns `{'port': '9090'}`
- `parse_directives('# only a comment\n\n')` returns `{}`

rewrites.rewrite:
ASCII Art Transformer

Implement `frame_ascii(art, width)`.

`art` is a multi-line string of ASCII art. Return the art with a box drawn around it: every line becomes `'|' + centered_line + '|'`, and a top and bottom border of the form `'+' + '-' * width + '+'` is added above and below. `width` is the total width of the framed output, so each content line is `width - 2` characters wide between the bars.

Rules:
- Centre each line inside `width - 2` characters. The left pad is `(width - 2 - len(line)) // 2` and the right pad is whatever is left over, so an odd remainder goes to the right.
- A line longer than `width - 2` is returned unchanged between the bars. Do not truncate it and do not wrap it; the output is then wider than `width` and that is the specified behaviour.
- Split `art` on newlines and keep empty lines as empty lines -- they still get bars and padding.
- A single trailing newline does not add an extra empty line of art.
- `width` must be at least 4. For smaller values, clamp it to 4 rather than raising.
- Return the string; do not print it.

Edge cases:
- `frame_ascii('', 10)` returns the two borders and nothing between them: `'+--------+\n+--------+'`. An empty `art` is not the same as an art string holding one empty line, which does get a row.
- An odd padding remainder always favours the right side.

Examples:
- `frame_ascii('hi', 8)` returns `'+------+\n|  hi  |\n+------+'`
- `frame_ascii('a\n\nb', 6)` returns `'+----+\n| a  |\n|    |\n| b  |\n+----+'`
- `frame_ascii('abcdefgh', 6)` returns `'+----+\n|abcdefgh|\n+----+'`

rewrites.rewrite:
Banner Formatter Pro

Implement `make_banner(text, width)`.

`text` is a single line of text. Return a three-line banner: a rule of `=` characters, the text centred in a line of the same width, and a second rule, joined by newlines. The rule is exactly `width` `=` characters with no leading or trailing characters.

Rules:
- The text line is exactly `width` characters. Pad with spaces: the left pad is `(width - len(text)) // 2` and the right pad is the remainder, so an odd remainder goes to the right.
- A multi-line `text` is treated as one line: split on newlines and use the first element. This problem does not wrap.
- If `text` is longer than `width`, do not truncate and do not wrap. Return the banner with the rule still `width` wide and the text line left unpadded and overhanging. State this in the test so the overhang is graded, not guessed at.
- `width` must be at least 1. Smaller values are clamped to 1.
- Return the string; do not print it.

Edge cases:
- `make_banner('', 7)` returns `'=======\n       \n======='` -- seven `=`, then seven spaces.
- An odd remainder favours the right-hand pad.

Examples:
- `make_banner('HELLO', 11)` returns `'===========\n   HELLO   \n==========='`
- `make_banner('hi', 6)` returns `'======\n  hi  \n======'`
- `make_banner('too long for me', 6)` returns `'======\ntoo long for me\n======'`

rewrites.rewrite:
Barcode Validator Pro

Implement `is_valid_barcode(code)`.

`code` is a candidate EAN-13 barcode as a string. Return `True` if it is a well-formed EAN-13 with a correct check digit, and `False` otherwise. Do not raise on any input.

Rules:
- The string must be exactly 13 characters and every character must be an ASCII digit `0`-`9`. Anything else -- wrong length, a letter, a space, a leading or trailing newline -- returns `False`.
- The first digit must not be `0`. A barcode starting with `0` is not a valid EAN-13 country prefix, so return `False`.
- The thirteenth digit is a modulo-10 check digit over the first twelve. Working from the left of those twelve, the digits in even positions (2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th, 10th, 12th) have weight 3 and the digits in odd positions (1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th, 9th, 11th) have weight 1. The check digit is `(10 - (weighted_sum % 10)) % 10` and must equal the thirteenth character.
- Empty string returns `False`. Return a bool, never a truthy string or a number.

Edge cases:
- `'4006381333931'` is valid.
- The same code with the last digit changed to anything else is not.
- `'0400638133393'` is rejected on the leading-zero rule even though its check digit is arithmetically consistent.
- `'400638133393'` (12 characters) returns `False` -- do not pad it.

Examples:
- `is_valid_barcode('4006381333931')` returns `True`
- `is_valid_barcode('4006381333930')` returns `False`
- `is_valid_barcode('5901234123457')` returns `True`
- `is_valid_barcode('40063813339')` returns `False`
- `is_valid_barcode('')` returns `False`

rewrites.notes: The grader's sandbox blocks the `base64` module outright (`BLOCKED_MODULES` in src/ducky/sandbox.py), so a rewrite that said 'use the base64 module' would be un-submittable. The rewrite therefore specifies the encoding itself and says why the standard library route is unavailable. This is the kind of constraint a generated description never carries and a student discovers only at grading time.
rewrites.rewrite:
Base64 Transformer

Implement `to_base64(text)`.

`text` is a string. Return its Base64 encoding as a string of ASCII characters, with no line breaks and no trailing newline.

Rules:
- The input is encoded as UTF-8 bytes first, so any character outside ASCII must survive the round trip: `to_base64('caf\u00e9')` returns `'Y2Fmw6k='`.
- The `base64` module is not available in this grading sandbox, so the alphabet and padding have to be implemented directly. The standard alphabet is `ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789+/`.
- Every three input bytes become four output characters. A trailing group of one byte becomes two characters plus `==`; a trailing group of two bytes becomes three characters plus a single `=`.
- The empty string returns `''`, not `'='`.
- Output uses `+` and `/`, never the URL-safe `-` and `_`.
- Return the encoded string; do not print it.

Edge cases:
- `to_base64('')` returns `''`.
- `to_base64('a')` returns `'YQ=='` and `to_base64('ab')` returns `'YWI='` -- the two padding cases.
- A string whose length is a multiple of 3 takes no padding at all.

Examples:
- `to_base64('Man')` returns `'TWFu'`
- `to_base64('Ma')` returns `'TWE='`
- `to_base64('M')` returns `'TQ=='`
- `to_base64('Hello, World!')` returns `'SGVsbG8sIFdvcmxkIQ=='`
- `to_base64('')` returns `''`

rewrites.notes: The stub returns the first argument. The rewrite fixes the brace depth rule for the field values, which is the only part of a BibTeX parser that is genuinely hard, and states which parts of BibTeX are deliberately out of scope so a student is not graded on `@string` macros.
rewrites.rewrite:
Bibtex Parser

Implement `parse_entry(entry)`.

`entry` is a single BibTeX entry as a string, for example `@article{knuth1984, title = {The TeXbook}, year = 1984}`. Return a dict with two kinds of key: the entry type under the key `'type'`, and every field under its own name, both lowercased. Do not raise on any input.

Rules:
- The first non-whitespace character must be `@`. Strip the leading `@`, then read the entry type up to the first `{`. Lowercase it.
- Read the citation key: everything up to the first top-level `,` or the closing `}`. Store it under `'key'`, lowercased and stripped. It is not a field.
- Each remaining item is `name = value`. Split on the first `=`; the name is lowercased and stripped.
- A field value is either a braced block or a bare token. When it is braced, the value is everything between the outermost braces, with the braces removed -- so a value may itself contain commas, `=` and braces. When it is unbraced, it runs to the next `,` at brace depth 0.
- Numeric values are converted with `int()` or `float()` when they parse as one; everything else stays a string. `'year'` therefore comes back as `1984`, not `'1984'`.
- Fields whose value is an empty braced block `{}` are omitted from the result rather than stored as `''`.
- Nested braces inside a value are returned as written, unbalanced outer braces are tolerated by treating the last `}` as the terminator.
- Out of scope, and therefore not graded: `@string` macro definitions, `@comment`, quoted (`"`) field values, and multiple entries in one string. If `entry` does not start with `@` or has no `{`, return `{}`.

Edge cases:
- `'@misc{key}'` returns `{'type': 'misc', 'key': 'key'}`.
- Whitespace and newlines between fields are insignificant.

Examples:
- `parse_entry('@Article{knuth1984, Title = {The TeXbook}, Year = 1984}')` returns `{'type': 'article', 'key': 'knuth1984', 'title': 'The TeXbook', 'year': 1984}`
- `parse_entry('@inproceedings{a, author = {Knuth, Donald E.}, booktitle = {TUG}, pages = {1--20}}')` returns `{'type': 'inproceedings', 'key': 'a', 'author': 'Knuth, Donald E.', 'booktitle': 'TUG', 'pages': '1--20'}`
- `parse_entry('@misc{k}')` returns `{'type': 'misc', 'key': 'k'}`
- `parse_entry('not an entry')` returns `{}`

rewrites.rewrite:
Binary Transformer

Implement `to_binary_string(n)`.

`n` is an integer. Return its 32-bit binary representation as a string of exactly 32 characters containing only `0` and `1`, most significant bit first, with no `0b` prefix, no underscores and no leading-zero stripping.

Rules:
- For `n >= 0`, the string is the ordinary base-2 representation of `n`, left-padded with `0` to 32 characters.
- For `n < 0`, return the two's-complement representation: add `2 ** 32` to `n`, then take the low 32 bits. `to_binary_string(-1)` is 32 ones and `to_binary_string(-2)` is 31 ones followed by a zero.
- `0` returns 32 zeros, not `'0'` and not `''`.
- The output length is fixed at 32 for every input in range, so a student can be checked with `len(result) == 32` before anything else.
- Inputs outside the signed 32-bit range (`n < -2**31` or `n >= 2**31`) are out of scope and are not tested.
- `bin()` and `format(n, 'b')` are both permitted; `n.bit_length()` alone is not, because it drops the leading zeros.
- Return the string; do not print it.

Edge cases:
- `to_binary_string(0)` returns `'00000000000000000000000000000000'`.
- `to_binary_string(1)` returns `'00000000000000000000000000000001'`.
- `to_binary_string(-1)` returns `'11111111111111111111111111111111'`.

Examples:
- `to_binary_string(5)` returns `'00000000000000000000000000000101'`
- `to_binary_string(255)` returns `'00000000000000000000000011111111'`
- `to_binary_string(-2)` returns `'11111111111111111111111111111110'`
- `to_binary_string(0)` returns `'00000000000000000000000000000000'`

rewrites.rewrite:
Bitcoin Address Validator Pro

Implement `is_valid_address(address)`.

`address` is a candidate Bitcoin address as a string. Return `True` if it is well-formed and passes its Base58Check checksum, and `False` otherwise. Do not raise on any input.

Rules:
- A mainnet P2PKH address is 26 to 35 characters inclusive. Anything outside that length returns `False`.
- Every character must be in the Base58 alphabet, which is the 58 characters `123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz`. The characters `0`, `O`, `I` and `l` are excluded on purpose: return `False` if any of them appears.
- The first character encodes the version byte and must be `1` for a mainnet P2PKH address. Any other first character returns `False`.
- The last four characters are a checksum: the first four bytes of the double SHA-256 of everything before them. Compute it with `hashlib.sha256(hashlib.sha256(payload).digest()).digest()` and compare the first four bytes to the last four characters decoded from Base58. `hashlib` is available in the grading sandbox; the `base64` module is not, so Base58 decoding has to be written out.
- To decode Base58, treat the string as a big-endian base-58 number: start from `0` and for each character multiply the running total by 58 and add that character's index in the alphabet, then convert the total to exactly 25 bytes big-endian. Do not pad to the length of the input string -- a 34-character address decodes to 25 bytes, and padding to 34 corrupts the checksum. A number too large for 25 bytes returns `False` rather than raising.
- Return `False` for the empty string, and `False` rather than an exception for any string containing a character outside the alphabet.

Edge cases:
- A 26-character string of valid Base58 characters that starts with `1` but whose checksum is wrong returns `False` -- the length and alphabet rules are not sufficient.
- Changing any single character of a valid address invalidates the checksum, so it returns `False`.
- A testnet address starting with `m` or `n` is out of scope for this problem and is not tested.

Examples:
- `is_valid_address('1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa')` returns `True`
- `is_valid_address('1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNb')` returns `False` -- one character changed, checksum broken, and the length and alphabet rules still pass
- `is_valid_address('0A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa')` returns `False` -- `0` is not in the Base58 alphabet, and the check must happen before decoding so this returns `False` instead of raising
- `is_valid_address('')` returns `False`
